definition: An extinct marine animal with a spiral shell, common fossils from the Mesozoic Era.
An animal that walks on two legs, like T-Rex and Velociraptor.
A meat-eating animal. Many theropod dinosaurs were fierce carnivores.
Fossilized dinosaur poop! Scientists study these to learn what dinosaurs ate.
The last period of the Mesozoic Era (145–66 million years ago). Ended with the asteroid impact.
The scientific name for the group of all dinosaurs, coined by Richard Owen in 1842.
When every member of a species dies out. Non-bird dinosaurs went extinct 66 million years ago.
Preserved remains or traces of ancient life found in rock. Can be bones, teeth, footprints, or even eggs!
Stones swallowed by dinosaurs to help grind food in their stomachs — like a built-in blender!
A plant-eating animal. Sauropods and ceratopsians were herbivores.
A marine reptile that looked like a dolphin. Not a dinosaur, but lived alongside them!
The middle period of the Mesozoic Era (201–145 million years ago). The age of giant sauropods!
The geological boundary marking the mass extinction event 66 million years ago that ended the dinosaurs.
The 'Age of Reptiles' — the era spanning 252–66 million years ago, divided into Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous.
An animal that eats both plants and meat. Some dinosaurs like Oviraptor were likely omnivores.
A scientist who studies ancient life through fossils. They're real-life dinosaur detectives!
Flying reptiles that lived alongside dinosaurs. They were NOT dinosaurs, but close relatives!
An animal that walks on four legs, like Triceratops and Stegosaurus.
Short for dromaeosaurid — a family of feathered, fast-running predatory dinosaurs.
Giant long-necked, plant-eating dinosaurs like Brachiosaurus and Argentinosaurus — the largest land animals ever!
Two-legged, mostly carnivorous dinosaurs. Includes T-Rex, Velociraptor, and modern birds!
The first period of the Mesozoic Era (252–201 million years ago). When dinosaurs first appeared!
A single bone in the spine. Some sauropod vertebrae were over 3 feet long!
